title: "Milestones"
subtitle: "How we got from early neural networks to today's language models and agents: a selective timeline for locating the course's ideas in time"
toc-depth: 2
---

*This page is a selective intellectual timeline, not a history of
artificial intelligence. It makes no claim to completeness. Each entry
was chosen because it helps place a concept taught in this course in
time; many famous systems, and many important lines of work, are left
out because the course does not depend on them. Dates are those of the
cited publication: an arXiv first posting, a journal issue, or a dated
article. Where a paper was revised later, the entry says so.*

*A note on wording. The history of this field is full of overlapping
antecedents, and "first", "invented", and "discovered" are rarely safe.
This page therefore says what a cited source did and how it described
itself, and it uses words such as "became influential" or "helped
establish" rather than asserting priority. Where a paper's own abstract
calls its method new, the entry quotes that self-description rather
than endorsing it.* [S-74]

## What the timeline should make clear

Read as a whole, the entries below support seven points that are easy
to get wrong from the outside.

- **Neural networks substantially predate language models.** Learning
  machines built from adjustable units were being studied in the 1950s.
- **Backpropagation did not arrive with transformers.** The
  loss-gradient-update loop this course works by hand was influential
  in neural-network training by the mid-1980s.
- **A transformer is a neural-network architecture, not the beginning of
  neural networks.** It is built from the same units, layers, and
  training procedure as its predecessors, arranged differently.
- **Attention had important precursors before 2017.** A learned,
  weighted selection over input positions was used in translation
  systems several years before the Transformer made it the whole
  architecture.
- **Large pretrained models required more than the architecture.** The
  practice of pretraining once and reusing, the effect of scale, and
  very large text corpora were separate developments.
- **Post-training and agent systems are later layers.** They sit on top
  of, or around, a pretrained model; neither is a new kind of network.
- **Today's systems are the result of several interacting lines of
  work**, not one isolated invention. [S-74]

## Neural networks before language models

### 1958 · The perceptron {#m-1958}

**What changed.** Frank Rosenblatt's paper in *Psychological Review*
developed the perceptron, described in its title as "a probabilistic
model for information storage and organization in the brain", as a
hypothetical learning system. [S-64] The 1986 backpropagation paper
listed below names the "perceptron-convergence procedure" as an
"earlier, simpler" learning method than its own, which locates the
perceptron as an ancestor of the training loop this course teaches.
[S-65]

**Why it matters here.** The basic object of the neural-networks lesson,
a unit that forms a weighted sum and passes it through a nonlinearity,
is decades older than any language model. Nothing in the perceptron
involves language; it is here to fix the starting point.

**In the course:** [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
§3–§5.

**Source:** Rosenblatt, F. (1958), "The perceptron: A probabilistic
model for information storage and organization in the brain",
*Psychological Review* 65(6), 386–408,
<https://doi.org/10.1037/h0042519>. The entry describes the paper by
its title and by how the 1986 paper characterizes it; it does not
summarize the paper's own mechanism. [S-64]

### 1986 · Backpropagation becomes practically influential {#m-1986}

**What changed.** Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams described in *Nature*
what their abstract calls "a new learning procedure, back-propagation,
for networks of neurone-like units", which "repeatedly adjusts the
weights of the connections in the network so as to minimize a measure
of the difference between the actual output vector of the net and the
desired output vector", so that hidden units "come to represent
important features of the task domain". [S-65]

**Why it matters here.** This is the loss, gradient, and update loop the
course works through on a single unit, and this influential 1986
formulation predates the Transformer by more than three decades. Two
precisions. The course makes no claim about who first derived the
gradient computation; the paper is listed for the importance of its
formulation, and its "new" is the abstract's own word. And the 1986
paper uses "back-propagation" more broadly, for the whole learning
procedure that adjusts weights, whereas this course uses
backpropagation specifically for the gradient computation and reserves
the update for the optimizer. [S-14]

**In the course:** [Neurons, Layers, and Learning](learn/neural-networks.qmd)
§8–§10.

**Source:** Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., and Williams, R. J. (1986),
"Learning representations by back-propagating errors", *Nature* 323,
533–536, <https://www.nature.com/articles/323533a0>.

### 1997 · Long short-term memory {#m-1997}

**What changed.** Hochreiter and Schmidhuber addressed a known
difficulty in training recurrent networks to use information across
long time intervals, which their abstract attributes to "insufficient,
decaying error back flow", by introducing what the abstract calls "a
novel, efficient, gradient-based method called 'Long Short-Term
Memory' (LSTM)". The paper reviews earlier recurrent-network work at
length and builds on an earlier analysis of the problem. [S-66]

**Why it matters here.** Recurrent networks, and LSTM in particular,
were the established approach to sequence modeling that the Transformer
paper compared itself against two decades later. [S-21] The sequential
dependency the course uses to motivate self-attention is a property of
this family: each step's summary waits for the previous one.

**In the course:** [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §1–§2.

**Source:** Hochreiter, S., and Schmidhuber, J. (1997), "Long Short-Term
Memory", *Neural Computation* 9(8), 1735–1780,
<https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735>; author-hosted copy at
<https://www.bioinf.jku.at/publications/older/2604.pdf>.

## Learning representations of language

### 2003 · A neural probabilistic language model {#m-2003}

**What changed.** Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Jauvin proposed to
"learn simultaneously a distributed representation for each word along
with the probability function for word sequences": each word is mapped
to a learned vector through a table that is "a $|V| \times m$ matrix of
free parameters", and the network's parameters are tuned "to maximize
the log-likelihood of the training data". [S-29] [S-41]

**Why it matters here.** Two of the course's central objects are already
here: a learned embedding table, and next-token prediction trained by
maximum likelihood. The network is not a transformer and its vocabulary
is words rather than subword tokens, and the course does not claim this
was the first such model; it is a clear early statement of the
idea.

**In the course:** [From Text to Numbers](learn/how-created.qmd) §5;
[How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §3.

**Source:** Bengio, Y., Ducharme, R., Vincent, P., and Jauvin, C. (2003),
"A Neural Probabilistic Language Model", *Journal of Machine Learning
Research* 3, 1137–1155,
<https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf>.

### 2014 · Sequence-to-sequence learning {#m-2014}

**What changed.** Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le presented "a general
end-to-end approach to sequence learning" that "uses a multilayered
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to map the input sequence to a vector of a
fixed dimensionality, and then another deep LSTM to decode the target
sequence from the vector". [S-67]

**Why it matters here.** This is a recurrent network generating an
output sequence one token at a time from an encoded input, the
encoder–decoder shape that the Transformer later kept. The single
fixed-length vector between encoder and decoder is also the bottleneck
that the next entry addressed.

**In the course:** [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §1–§3.

**Source:** Sutskever, I., Vinyals, O., and Le, Q. V. (2014), "Sequence
to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks", arXiv:1409.3215 (v1
2014-09-10; v3 2014-12-14), <https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215>.

### 2014–2015 · Attention for neural translation {#m-2015-attention}

**What changed.** Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio conjectured "that the use of
a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of
this basic encoder-decoder architecture" and proposed "allowing a model
to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are
relevant to predicting a target word". The paper was posted in
September 2014 and, per its arXiv listing, accepted at ICLR 2015.
[S-68]

**Why it matters here.** A learned, weighted selection over input
positions, the mechanism now generally called attention, was in use
several years before the Transformer. The 2017 architecture's
contribution was to build the network from this mechanism rather than
to add it to a recurrent one. The abstract itself does not use the word
"attention".

**In the course:** [How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd)
§1–§2.

**Source:** Bahdanau, D., Cho, K., and Bengio, Y., "Neural Machine
Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate", arXiv:1409.0473
(v1 2014-09-01; v7 2016-05-19), <https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473>.

### 2015 · Subword vocabularies {#m-2015-subword}

**What changed.** Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch proposed making a
translation model "capable of open-vocabulary translation by encoding
rare and unknown words as sequences of subword units", using "a
segmentation based on the byte pair encoding compression algorithm".
[S-27]

**Why it matters here.** The paper helped establish subword
tokenization as a practical way to handle open vocabularies in neural
language systems, which is the reason a token in this course is often a
word fragment rather than a word. Modern tokenizers use several related
subword- and byte-based approaches, with their own rules about spaces
and punctuation, so the course treats this as an important step rather
than the unique origin of current tokenization.

**In the course:** [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§2–§4.

**Source:** Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., and Birch, A., "Neural Machine
Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units", arXiv:1508.07909 (posted
August 2015; v5 2016-06-10), <https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909>.

## The transformer, pretraining, and scale

### 2017 · The Transformer {#m-2017}

**What changed.** Vaswani and colleagues stated that the dominant
sequence-transduction models of the time were "based on complex
recurrent or convolutional neural networks", with LSTM and gated
recurrent networks "firmly established as state of the art", and
proposed an architecture built from attention and feed-forward layers
without recurrence, reporting it "superior in quality while being more
parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train" on the
two translation tasks tested. [S-21] Removing the sequential dependency
of recurrence is given as a central motivation. [S-16] [S-23]

**Why it matters here.** Transformer architectures became the dominant
foundation for many modern large language models, and the course's
why-transformers lesson is built around this paper's own comparison of
path lengths and sequential operations. Two cautions. The Transformer
is a neural-network architecture, assembled from the units, layers, and
training loop of the earlier entries. And its attention mechanism has
the 2014–2015 precursor above; the paper's defining architectural move
was to build sequence transduction around attention and feed-forward
computation rather than recurrence or convolution.

**In the course:** [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd);
[How Self-Attention Moves Information](learn/transformers-attention.qmd).

**Source:** Vaswani, A., et al. (2017), "Attention Is All You Need",
arXiv:1706.03762 (v1 2017-06-12; v7 2023-08-02),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>.

### 2018–2019 · Pretraining and transfer {#m-2018}

**What changed.** Three reports helped establish transformer
pretraining and transfer as a central recipe in natural-language
processing. Radford, Narasimhan, Salimans, and Sutskever (2018)
demonstrated "that large gains on these tasks can be realized by
generative pre-training of a language model on a diverse corpus of
unlabeled text, followed by discriminative fine-tuning on each specific
task", using a transformer in a two-stage procedure; the paper names
earlier pretrain-then-fine-tune work as its closest antecedent. [S-69]
Devlin and colleagues (BERT, 2018) reported that a pretrained
bidirectional transformer "can be fine-tuned with just one additional
output layer" for a wide range of tasks. [S-24] Radford and colleagues
(GPT-2, 2019) reported that language models "begin to learn these
tasks without any explicit supervision" when trained on a large corpus
of web text. [S-44]

**Why it matters here.** The three contributions are distinct:
generative pretraining followed by task fine-tuning; pretrained
bidirectional representations with light task adaptation; and task
behavior appearing without explicit task-specific supervision.
Together they show that large-scale pretraining, data, compute, and the
reuse of pretrained models were additional developments beyond the
Transformer architecture itself. GPT-2 is also the source of the
course's tokenizer figures.

**In the course:** [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §5;
[How Pretraining Works](learn/training.qmd) §6.

**Sources:** Radford, A., Narasimhan, K., Salimans, T., and Sutskever,
I., "Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training"
(OpenAI, 2018),
<https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf>.
Devlin, J., et al., "BERT: Pre-training of
Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding",
arXiv:1810.04805 (v1 2018-10-11; v2 2019-05-24),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>. Radford, A., et al., "Language
Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (OpenAI, 2019),
<https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf>.

### 2020 · Scale, and behavior from demonstrations in the input {#m-2020-scale}

**What changed.** Kaplan and colleagues reported that language-model
loss "scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the
amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more
than seven orders of magnitude". [S-25] Brown and colleagues reported
that GPT-3, "an autoregressive language model with 175 billion
parameters", could be applied "without any gradient updates or
fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via
text interaction", and that "scaling up language models greatly
improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance". [S-26]

**Why it matters here.** These results showed that scale, training
data, and inference-time demonstrations were important empirical
developments beyond the architecture itself. The second result shows
behavior being steered by inference-time context alone, with no
parameter change: the distinction between parameters and context that
runs through the whole course. Both are empirical findings for the
systems and setups studied; the course describes in-context behavior as
observed task performance, not as learning in the training sense.

**In the course:** [Why Transformers](learn/why-transformers.qmd) §5;
[Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd) §8.

**Sources:** Kaplan, J., et al., "Scaling Laws for Neural Language
Models", arXiv:2001.08361 (v1 2020-01-23),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361>. Brown, T., et al., "Language Models
are Few-Shot Learners", arXiv:2005.14165 (v4 2020-07-22),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>.

### 2020 · Retrieval-augmented generation {#m-2020-retrieval}

**What changed.** Lewis and colleagues observed that pretrained models'
"ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited"
and described models "which combine pre-trained parametric and
non-parametric memory for language generation", the non-parametric
memory being an index of retrievable text. [S-33]

**Why it matters here.** This became an influential formulation of
combining pretrained generation with retrieved external information.
Modern assistants and agents use a broader range of retrieval and
tool-based mechanisms; the course abstracts from the paper's specific
architecture, a learned retriever paired with a generator, to the
general idea of bringing external evidence into inference-time context,
where it changes the inputs to one call and not the parameters.

**In the course:** [Tokens, Embeddings, and the Context Window](learn/tokens-context.qmd)
§10; [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §7.

**Source:** Lewis, P., et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for
Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks", arXiv:2005.11401 (v4 2021-04-12),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401>.

## Post-training, tools, and agents

### 2022 · Chain-of-thought prompting {#m-2022-cot}

**What changed.** Wei and colleagues reported that "generating a chain of
thought -- a series of intermediate reasoning steps -- significantly
improves the ability of large language models to perform complex
reasoning", elicited by providing "a few chain of thought
demonstrations" in the prompt, with the effect appearing in
"sufficiently large" models. [S-70]

**Why it matters here.** It is an early, widely cited demonstration
that on some difficult tasks, generating intermediate reasoning tokens
provides additional inference-time computation and can improve
performance. Note what it is: a prompting technique, applied at
inference time, with no parameter change. The 2025 entry below is about
training models to produce such traces. The course treats generated
reasoning as output, not as a transcript of internal computation.

**In the course:** [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §7;
[Using Models Well](learn/using-models-well.qmd) §9.

**Source:** Wei, J., et al., "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits
Reasoning in Large Language Models", arXiv:2201.11903 (v1 2022-01-28;
v6 2023-01-10), <https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903>.

### 2022 · Instruction following from human feedback {#m-2022-instructgpt}

**What changed.** Ouyang and colleagues fine-tuned a pretrained model
first on "labeler demonstrations of the desired model behavior" with
supervised learning, then on "rankings of model outputs" using
reinforcement learning from human feedback, and reported that outputs
of their 1.3-billion-parameter post-trained model were preferred to
those of the 175-billion-parameter pretrained model. [S-46] The
preference-learning component builds on earlier reinforcement-learning
work in which a reward was learned from "human preferences between
pairs of trajectory segments" rather than specified by hand. [S-71]

**Why it matters here.** This is the post-training layer: parameter
updates after pretraining that shape a model into an assistant. The
course presents it as one provider's 2022 recipe and as one route
through a family of methods; "RLHF" names that route, not
post-training as a whole.

**In the course:** [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §3 and §5.

**Sources:** Ouyang, L., et al., "Training language models to follow
instructions with human feedback", arXiv:2203.02155 (v1 2022-03-04),
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155>. Christiano, P., et al., "Deep
reinforcement learning from human preferences", arXiv:1706.03741 (v1
2017-06-12; v4 2023-02-17), <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741>.

### 2022 · Reasoning traces interleaved with actions {#m-2022-react}

**What changed.** Yao and colleagues explored "the use of LLMs to
generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an
interleaved manner", where actions "allow it to interface with external
sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional
information", for example through a simple Wikipedia API. [S-72]

**Why it matters here.** The model, action, and observation loop this
course describes, in which the model generates a request, software
executes it, and the observation returns to the context for the next
step, closely resembles this pattern, and ReAct is an influential early
formulation of it in the language-model setting. It is not claimed as
the origin of agents; tool use and environment interaction have longer
histories the course does not trace.

**In the course:** [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §2 and §5.

**Source:** Yao, S., et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in
Language Models", arXiv:2210.03629 (v1 2022-10-06; v3 2023-03-10, the
ICLR camera-ready version), <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629>.

### 2023 · Direct preference optimization {#m-2023}

**What changed.** Rafailov and colleagues characterized the reward-model
route as "a complex and often unstable procedure" and proposed updating
the language model directly from preference pairs with a
classification-style loss, "eliminating the need for sampling from the
LM during fine-tuning", reporting results that matched or improved on
the reward-model route on the tasks tested. [S-47]

**Why it matters here.** It shows that preference-based post-training is
a family with more than one implementation, which is why the course
keeps "RLHF" and "post-training" apart. Both routes remain in use.

**In the course:** [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §5.

**Source:** Rafailov, R., et al., "Direct Preference Optimization: Your
Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model", arXiv:2305.18290 (v1
2023-05-29; v3 2024-07-29), <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290>.

### 2024 · Workflow versus agent {#m-2024}

**What changed.** An engineering article from Anthropic distinguished
workflows, "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through
predefined code paths", from agents, "systems where LLMs dynamically
direct their own processes and tool usage", recommended "finding the
simplest solution possible", and described the basic building block as
a model augmented with retrieval, tools, and memory. [S-50] As of this
course's access date, the article carries a note that much of the
tooling landscape it describes has changed since December 2024. [S-73]

**Why it matters here.** This is the engineering vocabulary the course
adopts for the last step of its story. It is engineering guidance, not
a scientific result and not a product launch, and the course states
that "agent" terminology is not universally standardized.

**In the course:** [From Assistant to Agent](learn/agents.qmd) §4.

**Source:** Anthropic, "Building effective agents", published
2024-12-19, accessed 2026-09-15,
<https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents>.

### 2025 · Reinforcement learning against checkable rewards {#m-2025}

**What changed.** The DeepSeek-R1 report stated that reasoning ability
"can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning (RL),
obviating the need for human-labeled reasoning trajectories", using
rule-based rewards on tasks whose answers can be checked; the resulting
model, R1-Zero, produced steadily longer reasoning traces but suffered
from poor readability and language mixing, and the released R1 was
trained through a multi-stage framework combining supervised
fine-tuning, rejection sampling, and reinforcement learning. [S-49]

**Why it matters here.** It provides a detailed, high-profile public
case in which reinforcement learning with rule-based, checkable rewards
produced increasingly long reasoning traces, and it is the reason the
course keeps R1-Zero (reinforcement learning without supervised
fine-tuning as a preliminary step) and R1 (a multi-stage recipe with
supervised stages and reinforcement learning) apart. It is one lab's
published recipe; other providers have published less, and the course
generalizes neither recipe to reasoning-oriented models as a class.
Producing reasoning traces was a trained behavior here, where the 2022
prompting entry elicited them at inference time.

**In the course:** [Post-training](learn/posttraining.qmd) §7.

**Source:** DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning
Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning", arXiv:2501.12948 (v1
2025-01-22; v2 2026-01-04), <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>.

## What this timeline leaves out

Several lines of development that mattered are absent because the
course does not build on them: the hardware and software that made
large training runs feasible; the construction and filtering of
training corpora; convolutional networks and the vision work that
shaped deep learning in the early 2010s; earlier word-vector methods;
alternatives to dense attention; open-weight model families; evaluation
methodology; and most of the commercial products through which people
meet these systems. Omission here is a statement about the course's
scope, not about importance. [S-74]

For the meaning of any term used above, see the [glossary](glossary.qmd).
For what to read next, see [resources](resources.qmd).
